Part 1: Source Code Analysis — Logistics Management Application

The aim of this analysis is to identify which design patterns are genuinely implemented in your FastAPI application, where the evidence appears in the source code, and what problems remain in the current design.

I inspected the Python backend in your uploaded WareHouseManagement-main.zip, focusing on the API modules, repositories, Pydantic models, database manager, and PRD. The findings below distinguish actual implementations from patterns that would only be suitable for future refactoring.

The application is a Warehouse & Transportation Management System (WTMS). It uses FastAPI for REST APIs, Pydantic for data validation, asyncpg for asynchronous PostgreSQL access, and React for the frontend.
The Pydantic models define input and output structures used by the API and repository layers.

Architecture finding: the backend follows a layered structure. However, the separation is not perfectly consistent: some API modules use FastAPI's dependency system to obtain repositories, while others directly use a shared database instance.
The API exposes operations for creating, listing, retrieving, updating and deactivating warehouses. It also manages zones, bins and warehouse utilization.
A route receives the repository through:
The repository contains methods such as create_warehouse(), get_warehouse_by_id(), get_all_warehouses(), update_warehouse() and delete_warehouse().
Repository Pattern: warehouse SQL operations are encapsulated in WarehouseRepository.
Dependency Injection: FastAPI Depends() supplies the repository and database dependency.
Layered Architecture: HTTP endpoints delegate data operations to the repository.
DTO-like models: Pydantic models separate create, update and response data.
The API checks that a warehouse exists before creating a zone, but this does not by itself guarantee that all related business rules are enforced.
Multi-warehouse selection based on distance, cost or stock availability is not implemented as a pluggable strategy.
The repository uses direct SQL, so database access and SQL details remain closely coupled to PostgreSQL and asyncpg.
The inventory module supports stock lookup, stock updates, inbound and outbound movements, transfers between warehouses, movement history and low-stock alerts.
The strongest evidence is the transactional transfer implementation:
The source inventory row is locked using SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, and the transaction updates both the source and destination inventory.
Repository Pattern: InventoryRepository encapsulates inventory data access.
Dependency Injection: the inventory API obtains its repository through Depends().
Transactional design: related stock operations are executed within a database transaction.
DTO-like models: separate Pydantic classes represent inventory operations, transfer movements and responses.
The transactional behavior is real, but there is no explicit UnitOfWork class. We should describe it as transaction management rather than claiming a formal Unit of Work implementation.
Concurrency is considered through row locking, but correctness also depends on database constraints and the handling of every stock-update path.
Inventory logic is concentrated in a repository rather than separated into a dedicated inventory service/domain layer. This can make business rules harder to reuse independently of the database.
The order API supports customer creation and listing, order creation, order listing and retrieving an order by ID.
Here, db is imported directly from app.database.
Repository Pattern: OrderRepository encapsulates customer and order database operations.
Layered Architecture: order endpoints delegate to the repository.
DTO-like models: CustomerCreate, OrderCreate and response models represent API data.
Unlike the warehouse and inventory modules, the order module does not obtain the database through Depends(get_db). It imports the shared db instance and constructs the repository directly.
This is still a repository implementation, but dependency injection is applied inconsistently.
The API catches broad Exception types and returns HTTP 400 in create operations. This can classify unexpected server or database failures as client errors.
The current API surface does not expose a full order lifecycle workflow, even though the PRD mentions updating order statuses.
We should inspect the complete create_order() transaction behavior before concluding whether creating an order and its items is atomic.

The main repository is named TransportationRepository, and its constructor accepts a Database object:
It contains methods for vehicle, driver, route and shipment operations.
Repository Pattern: transportation-related database access is encapsulated in TransportationRepository.
Layered Architecture: the API delegates persistence to the repository.
DTO-like models: separate Pydantic models represent vehicles, drivers, routes and shipments.
Major design limitation: the repository has too many responsibilities
TransportationRepository handles vehicles, drivers, routes and shipments in one class. These are related business concepts, but they do not necessarily have the same rules or reasons to change.
For example, adding a delivery partner integration should not require modifying unrelated vehicle CRUD operations.
This is a refactoring proposal, not a description of classes that already exist.

Like the order module, it imports the global database instance directly. This makes the implementation less consistent with the dependency-injection approach used in the warehouse and inventory modules.

This provides a basic representation of shipment progress.
Shipment status, planned and actual departure/arrival times, and shipment listing.
Not found in the inspected implementation: live tracking
No GPS coordinate stream, tracking-event API, WebSocket updates or observer-based notification mechanism was found in these shipment modules.
The PRD also identifies real-time GPS tracking as out of scope for Phase 1.
Observer Pattern: no explicit mechanism was found that subscribes multiple listeners to shipment-status or location changes.
State Pattern: a status field exists, but no state-specific classes or transition objects were found.
Event-driven architecture: no event publisher/subscriber mechanism was found in these modules.
The inspected transportation API exposes shipment creation and listing, but no dedicated endpoint for retrieving a shipment's full tracking history.
There is no separate shipment-tracking event model in the inspected Python model files.
A string status field does not, by itself, enforce valid status transitions.
Actual timestamps are data fields, not proof that the system automatically updates tracking information.
These findings give us a strong starting point for adding real-time tracking in Part 2.
The repository provides create_route() and get_all_routes(). The Pydantic module also defines RouteUpdate, but the inspected API does not expose a corresponding route-update endpoint.
Routes are stored as origin, destination, distance and estimated duration. There is no demonstrated multi-stop route graph or route optimization engine.
The existence of RouteUpdate does not mean route updating is implemented in the API.
Shipments refer to a route_id, but no strategy interface selects between shortest, fastest, cheapest or traffic-aware routes.
Dynamic rerouting and notifying affected customers are not implemented in the inspected modules.
This makes route management another strong candidate for a Strategy Pattern refactoring.

One academic distinction matters here: Repository is a recognizable design pattern, while Dependency Injection is a design technique and Layered Architecture is an architectural pattern. Pydantic models are DTO-like structures, and database transactions are a transactional mechanism. They should not all be presented as equivalent GoF patterns.
These are the issues I would prioritize in your analysis.

Suggestion: standardize dependency providers and use FastAPI dependency overrides for testing.
Evidence: one class manages vehicles, drivers, routes and shipments.
Suggestion: separate repositories and introduce a service layer for transportation business rules.
Evidence: shipment status and timestamps exist, but live GPS updates and tracking events were not found in the inspected modules.
Suggestion: introduce tracking events, a tracking service and an Observer-style notification mechanism.
Problem 4 — Route selection is not extensible
Evidence: routes contain static distance and duration fields; no route-selection interface was found.
Suggestion: introduce the Strategy Pattern for shortest, fastest, lowest-cost and traffic-aware routing.
Problem 5 — Delivery partner integration is not abstracted
Evidence: no delivery-partner interface or partner-specific adapter was found in the inspected transportation modules.
Suggestion: define a common delivery-partner interface and use adapters for external partner APIs. A factory can select the appropriate integration.
Problem 6 — Status and error handling need stronger rules
Evidence: shipment status is a string, and several create endpoints catch broad exceptions.
Suggestion: validate legal status transitions and map known database/domain errors to appropriate HTTP responses.
These are source-based observations, not proof that the entire application lacks every capability. In particular, the tracking and partner-integration findings apply to the inspected backend modules.
We should not introduce every pattern just to increase the pattern count. Each pattern should solve an identified design problem.

High-level nature: Fleetbase is an open-source, modular “logistics and supply chain operating system” (AGPL-3.0 / commercial dual-licensed). The top-level fleetbase/fleetbase repo is a meta-repo/orchestrator — it doesn’t contain most business logic itself. It stitches together ~14 independent git submodules (each its own GitHub repo) via .gitmodules, plus Docker/deploy tooling.

api/ — a thin Laravel 10 “shell” app. Its composer.json requires all backend logic as Composer packages (fleetbase/core-api, fleetbase/fleetops-api, fleetbase/ai, fleetbase/storefront-api, fleetbase/ledger-api, fleetbase/customer-portal-api, fleetbase/registry-bridge, plus closed-source valhalla-api/vroom-api routing engines). Its own app/ is nearly empty.

console/ — the Ember.js frontend shell. Its package.json pulls every module in as an installable Ember Engine (fleetops-engine, storefront-engine, ledger-engine, iam-engine, dev-engine, ai-engine, customer-portal-engine, registry-bridge-engine).
packages/ — git submodules for each module (empty until cloned).
docker/, docker-compose.yml, builds/, infra/helm — self-hosting/deployment tooling (8 compose services: cache, database, socket, scheduler, queue, console, application, httpd/Caddy).
database.mmd / erd.svg — full auto-generated ER diagram.
Module pattern (repeats across fleetops, storefront, pallet, ledger, ai, customer-portal, registry-bridge)
Each module submodule is a single repo containing both halves:
server/src/ (Laravel package: Models/, Http/Controllers/{Api,Internal}/v1/, Jobs/, Events/, Listeners/, Observers/, Notifications/, Mail/, Traits/, config, migrations, seeders, tests)
addon/ + app/ (Ember Engine: components/, controllers/, routes/, services/, models/, serializers/, templates/, translations)

ember-core/ember-ui and core-api/iam-engine/dev-engine are the shared foundations (iam-engine and dev-engine have no separate server/, since core-api already houses Users/Roles/Permissions/ApiCredentials/Webhooks).

Base Model (Fleetbase\Models\Model): UUID primary keys + parallel human-readable public_id, soft deletes, findById/findByIdOrFail (auto-detects UUID vs public_id), plus traits for caching, filtering, expandable relations.

Generic CRUD via HasApiControllerBehavior trait: controllers resolve their Model/Resource/Request/Filter class by naming convention and expose queryRecord, findRecord, createRecord, updateRecord, deleteRecord, bulkDelete — this is the backbone of nearly all ~100+ controllers.
Two route trees: public v1 (external API, fleetbase.api/fleetbase.platform-api middleware, API-key auth) vs internal int/v1 (console-only, session/Sanctum auth).

Domain-rich Models in fleetops: Order (2000+ lines), Driver, Vehicle, Payload, Waypoint, Fleet, Place, ServiceArea/Zone, Manifest, WorkOrder, telematics/fuel-provider models, inspections, purchase/service rates.

Order lifecycle is event-driven: OrderDispatched, OrderDriverAssigned, OrderCompleted, OrderCanceled, WaypointCompleted, GeofenceEntered/Exited/Dwelled, handled by matching Listeners/Handle* classes and Observers/*Observer for model hooks; async work goes through Jobs/ (ProcessAllocationJob, SyncTelematicDevicesJob, PollTelematicTelemetry, etc.).
Configurable workflow engine: Flow/ (Activity, Condition, Event, Logic, FlowResource) drives Fleet-Ops’ custom order activity flows.

Orchestration/dispatch: Orchestration/Engines/ — pluggable GreedyOrchestrationEngine, VroomOrchestrationEngine, DriverAssignmentEngine, RouteSequencingEngine, CapacityAllocationEngine behind an OrchestrationEngineInterface.
Tracking: Tracking/Providers/ — OsrmTrackingProvider, GoogleRoutesTrackingProvider, CalculatedTrackingProvider behind TrackingProviderInterface, managed by a TrackingProviderRegistry.

Auth: Sanctum-based, custom OAuth (Auth/OAuth/Drivers/ for Google, GitHub, Microsoft, Apple), RBAC via Role/Permission/Policy/Group models, webhook signing/delivery pipeline (Webhook/Signer, BackoffStrategy).
Ember Octane app using an Engines pattern for modularity; each business module ships as a lazily-loadable engine.

ember-core’s universe.js service is the extension/plugin host: decomposed into ExtensionManager (lazy engine loading), RegistryService, MenuService, WidgetService, HookService — this is what powers the “install extensions from the marketplace” system and lets modules register menu items, dashboard widgets, and hooks into the shell.

113 migrations in core-api (users, companies, roles/permissions, groups, files, API credentials, webhooks, chat, activity log, transactions) + 165 in fleetops-server (orders, drivers, vehicles, payloads, waypoints, geofences, telematics, fuel, inspections, maintenance, service rates, etc.), plus additional migrations per-module (storefront, ledger, pallet, ai, customer-portal, registry-bridge).

Relevant classes/interfaces: TrackingProviderInterface (contract: key(), capabilities(), canTrack(), track()); concrete implementations OsrmTrackingProvider, GoogleRoutesTrackingProvider, CalculatedTrackingProvider; context TrackingProviderManager; lookup TrackingProviderRegistry.
Participants in the pattern: Context = TrackingProviderManager::track(); Strategy interface = TrackingProviderInterface; ConcreteStrategies = the three provider classes.

How the classes interact: TrackingProviderManager never references a concrete provider class. It resolves a provider by string key from TrackingProviderRegistry::get($key), checks provider->canTrack($context), then calls provider->track($context, $options) — always through the interface type.
Important methods: TrackingProviderManager::track(), providerOrder(); TrackingProviderRegistry::register()/get(); each provider’s track()/canTrack().

Source-code evidence: TrackingProviderManager::track() loops foreach ($this->providerOrder($options) as $providerKey) { $provider = $this->registry->get($providerKey); ... $provider->track($context, $options); } — the variable $provider is only ever type-hinted/used as TrackingProviderInterface.

Why this is genuinely the pattern: There is a real interface, three real independent implementations that all satisfy it, and a Context class that is coded against the interface only and selects the concrete implementation at runtime (from config/settings), exactly matching Strategy’s structural definition — not just “multiple providers that happen to exist.”
What problem it solves: Lets the routing/ETA algorithm be swapped (OSRM vs Google Routes vs a pure haversine calculation) without touching the code that consumes tracking data.

Relevant classes/interfaces: OrchestrationEngineInterface (allocate(), getName(), getIdentifier()); GreedyOrchestrationEngine, VroomOrchestrationEngine, CapacityAllocationEngine (all implements OrchestrationEngineInterface).
Participants in the pattern: Context = OrchestrationController::run(); Strategy interface = OrchestrationEngineInterface; ConcreteStrategies = the three implements-confirmed engines.

How the classes interact: OrchestrationController is constructed with OrchestrationEngineRegistry $registry (injected), reads a setting fleetops.orchestrator_engine, calls $engine = $this->registry->resolve($engineId); $result = $engine->allocate($orders, $vehicles, $options); — the controller never names a concrete engine class for this branch.
Important methods: OrchestrationController::run(); OrchestrationEngineRegistry::register()/resolve(); each engine’s allocate().

Why this is genuinely the pattern: Confirmed via implements on all three classes, a shared method signature, and a Context that resolves the concrete strategy dynamically by string identifier read from a runtime setting.

What problem it solves: Lets an operator choose between a free built-in greedy heuristic and an external VROOM optimization solver without changing controller code, and lets third parties register new engines ($registry->register(new MyEngine()), documented directly in the interface’s docblock).

Benefit in Fleetbase: Orchestrator Workbench can fall back from VROOM (external service, may be down) to the built-in greedy engine at runtime — the 503 handler in run() explicitly suggests this fallback to the admin.

The fixed algorithm — extract payload → fill session attributes → [hook: onBefore] → static::create($input) → [hook: onAfter] → refresh/eager-load → mutate/return — never changes. Individual controllers (e.g. Internal/v1/OrderController::onAfterUpdate($request, $order)) supply only the hook body.

Source-code evidence: private function getControllerCallback(string $name): ?\Closure { if (method_exists($this, $name)) { return function (...$args) use ($name) { return $this->{$name}(...$args); }; } return null; } — reflection-based hook lookup is the textbook Template Method “primitive operation” mechanism.

Why this is genuinely the pattern: One invariant algorithm lives in the base trait; subclasses supply only the customizable steps (onBeforeCreate, onAfterUpdate, etc.) without re-implementing validation, session-attribute filling, eager-loading, or response shaping.
What problem it solves: Avoids duplicating the create/update/query/delete boilerplate across ~100+ controllers spanning core-api, fleetops, and pallet.

Benefit in Fleetbase, per area: Order uses onAfterUpdate to run activity/status side effects; WorkOrder/Warehouse fully override createRecord() while still delegating to the same underlying createRecordFromRequest() skeleton with an inline $onAfter closure (e.g. WarehouseController::createRecord() builds the Section/Aisle/Rack/Bin tree inside the $onAfter closure it passes in); Inventory/StockAdjustment use the skeleton unmodified.
Relevant classes/interfaces: constructor/method parameter type-hints resolved by Laravel’s service container.

Participants in the pattern: Dependents = OrchestrationController, TrackingIntelligenceService, TrackingProviderManager, ProcessAllocationJob; Dependencies injected = OrchestrationEngineRegistry, TrackingContextBuilder+TrackingProviderManager, TrackingProviderRegistry.

How the classes interact: None of these classes call new OrchestrationEngineRegistry() or new TrackingProviderRegistry() themselves — the container supplies the (singleton, per binding) instance based on the type-hint.

Important methods: OrchestrationController::__construct(protected OrchestrationEngineRegistry $registry); TrackingIntelligenceService::__construct(protected TrackingContextBuilder $contextBuilder, protected TrackingProviderManager $providerManager); ProcessAllocationJob::handle(OrchestrationEngineRegistry $registry) (method injection — Laravel resolves job handle() parameters from the container too).
Source-code evidence: public function __construct(protected OrchestrationEngineRegistry $registry) {} — constructor-promoted, type-hinted, no manual instantiation anywhere in the class.

Why this is genuinely the pattern: Dependencies are declared as typed parameters and resolved externally, not constructed internally — the textbook DI structural requirement — and this is what makes the Strategy/Registry pattern above swappable/testable (a test can bind a fake OrchestrationEngineRegistry into the container).

What problem it solves: Decouples orchestration/tracking classes from the concrete construction of their collaborators, and is what allows the Strategy registries to be extended by third-party service providers ($this->app->resolving(OrchestrationEngineRegistry::class, function ($registry) { $registry->register(new MyEngine()); }), per the interface’s own docblock).
Benefit in Fleetbase: Extension developers can register new orchestration engines or tracking providers from their own service provider without modifying FleetOps’ core classes.

Observer — Delivery/Tracking, both variants genuinely present: Eloquent model observers (OrderObserver, PayloadObserver, TrackingNumberObserver, WorkOrderObserver bound via FleetOpsServiceProvider::$observers) and Laravel event/listener pub-sub (EventServiceProvider::$listen, one event → multiple independent listeners).
Composite — Delivery (Flow\Activity recursive single-class tree, uniform API at any depth).
Template Method — Cross-cutting across all six areas via HasApiModelBehavior::createRecordFromRequest/updateRecordFromRequest and HasApiControllerBehavior’s hook-resolution (getControllerCallback).
Command — Shipment (FinalizeApiOrderCreation/FinalizeInternalOrderCreation) and Route Management (ProcessAllocationJob) — Laravel Jobs implementing ShouldQueue with a handle() receiver method.

Dependency Injection — Tracking and Route Management (OrchestrationController, TrackingIntelligenceService, ProcessAllocationJob::handle() all receive collaborators via typed constructor/method parameters resolved by the container).

Service Layer — Business logic for Tracking (TrackingIntelligenceService, TrackingContextBuilder) and Route Management (OrchestrationEngineRegistry, the engines) is factored into standalone Support/Tracking/Orchestration classes rather than living in controllers or models — a genuine service layer, distinct from the more “fat-model” pattern used by plain-CRUD areas like Warehouse/Inventory.

Event-Driven Architecture — Confirmed at the framework level: domain events (OrderDispatched, OrderCompleted, GeofenceEntered, etc.) are dispatched by models/controllers and consumed asynchronously by decoupled listeners, several of which (SendResourceLifecycleWebhook) further propagate to external systems via webhooks.

MVC-inspired API layering — Backend: Eloquent Model → Controller (HasApiControllerBehavior) → API Resource (Http/Resources/v1/Order.php etc., the “View”/serialization layer) → JSON. Frontend: Ember’s own Route/Controller/Template convention. Not classic desktop MVC, but the Model/Controller/Resource split is real and consistently applied.

Registry (Service Locator variant) — OrchestrationEngineRegistry and TrackingProviderRegistry are both plain runtime lookup tables (register()/resolve()/get()) that make the Strategy pattern above extensible by third parties. Not one of the named GoF patterns in the prompt, but structurally real and worth naming.

Trait-based cross-cutting composition — HasUuid, HasPublicId, HasApiModelBehavior, SendsWebhooks, TracksApiCredential, etc. are PHP traits mixed into nearly every model across all six areas. This is horizontal code reuse (PHP’s mechanism for mixins), not a GoF pattern, but it is the dominant reuse mechanism in the codebase and underlies the Template Method finding above.

Single Table Inheritance (Fowler, not GoF) — Warehouse extends Place, Pallet\Product extends Entity. A genuine, named architectural pattern (from Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture), but it is not one of the GoF patterns requested, so it is called out here rather than mis-labeled as Adapter/Decorator.
C. FEATURES THAT RESEMBLE A PATTERN BUT ARE NOT ENOUGH TO CLAIM THE PATTERN

“State” pattern for Order status — Order has a status string column and the Flow/Activity/Condition/Logic classes evaluate JSON-configured rules against it. This resembles State (different behavior per status) but there is no OrderState interface with one concrete class per status implementing polymorphic behavior — it is a data-driven rule interpreter (switch statements over operator/type strings in Condition::eval() and Logic::passes()), not the GoF State pattern. Should not be reported as State.

“Builder” pattern for Payload::setEntities()/setWaypoints() — These methods return $this and construct related records step-by-step, which superficially looks like Builder’s fluent interface. But there is no separate Builder class, no Director, no swappable builder implementations, and no distinct Product class assembled externally — Payload mutates its own related tables directly. This is a fluent/method-chaining API on the model itself, not GoF Builder.

“Composite” for the Warehouse Section→Aisle→Rack→Bin hierarchy — Structurally this is just a chain of independent Eloquent models (WarehouseSection, WarehouseAisle, WarehouseRack, WarehouseBin) connected by ordinary belongsTo/hasMany foreign keys, each extending the generic base Model with no shared “Component” interface or uniform recursive method (no WarehouseNode::totalCapacity() implemented polymorphically at every level, for example). This is a relational parent-child hierarchy, not Composite. (Contrast with Flow\Activity, which genuinely qualifies — see Section A — because it is one recursive class with a uniform API.)

“Repository” pattern — No dedicated Repository classes exist anywhere in the Shipment/Warehouse/Delivery/Tracking/Inventory/Route Management code (grep -ril Repository in fleetops/pallet returns nothing relevant; the only *Repository class in the whole codebase is OAuthConfigRepository, which belongs to Auth, outside these six areas). All data access in these six areas goes directly through Eloquent (Active Record), not through a Repository abstraction. Do not report Repository as present.

“Adapter” for Warehouse extends Place / Product extends Entity — This is inheritance-based specialization (Single Table Inheritance, see Section B), not Adapter. Adapter requires converting between two incompatible interfaces; here Warehouse simply is-a Place with additional relations, fully compatible with everything that already consumes Place. Labeling this Adapter would be a naming-based misclassification.

“Chain of Responsibility” for the tracking-provider fallback loop — TrackingProviderManager::track() iterates a list [primary, ...fallbacks] and tries each provider until one succeeds. This resembles Chain of Responsibility (a request passed along a chain until handled), but in true Chain of Responsibility each handler holds a reference to the next handler and decides itself whether to pass the request on. Here, the manager (not the providers) owns and walks the entire ordered list — the providers themselves have no knowledge of a “next” provider. This is more accurately “Strategy selected via an ordered fallback list inside the Context,” and should not be reported as Chain of Responsibility.
Which Verified Patterns Are Strongest, and Why
The strongest, most rigorously verifiable patterns are Strategy (Tracking and Route Management) and Template Method (cross-cutting HasApiModelBehavior).

Strategy is strongest because both instances satisfy every structural element without exception: a real interface keyword contract (TrackingProviderInterface, OrchestrationEngineInterface), multiple classes that genuinely implements it (confirmed by direct grep, not inference), and a Context class (TrackingProviderManager, OrchestrationController) that is provably coded against the interface type alone — the resolving code ($this->registry->resolve($engineId)) has no compile-time or runtime dependency on which concrete class it gets back.

Template Method is strongest because it is the single most load-bearing piece of architecture in the entire application — verified not just in one controller but as the shared mechanism underlying every one of the six areas’ create/update endpoints, with the hook-resolution mechanism (getControllerCallback) directly visible in source and directly exercised by name (onAfterUpdate, onBeforeCreate) in multiple real controllers (OrderController, WarehouseController).

These are strongest specifically because the evidence did not require any interpretive leap — the interface/abstract-skeleton existed as literal PHP language constructs (interface, implements, abstract) and the polymorphic call sites were found and quoted directly, rather than inferred from naming conventions or the mere presence of multiple similar classes. Patterns like Observer and Command are also solidly verified, but they rely partly on Laravel-framework-provided mechanics (event dispatcher, queue system) rather than being hand-rolled Fleetbase abstractions, which is why they are reported with slightly more framework-attribution context.
